vignette:
Martha is an 80-year-old woman who lives in a small town with her husband of fifty-three years. She spent her entire adult life as a midwife, delivering babies in the village and later at the district clinic. Even after formal retirement, families still call her when a labor is difficult or when a mother is afraid. For decades, her hands were steady, her voice calm, her presence a kind of certainty in the chaos of birth. That was before the accident.

The trauma happened two years ago, on a moonless night in the rainy season. A young woman’s labor had turned urgent—breech, cord prolapse, the words still make Martha’s chest tighten. She drove herself, as she always did, along the unpaved road that skirts the gully. She remembers the headlights picking out the rain, the mud, the sudden glare of a lorry swerving into her lane. She remembers the impact, the sickening lurch of the car rolling, the roof crumpling toward her face. Then a long silence, broken by the sound of her own breathing and the smell of petrol.

She was trapped for nearly an hour before a passing farmer heard her cries. The young mother was transferred to another midwife. The baby survived, but Martha does not know that for certain. She never asked. The thought of calling the family, of hearing the details, makes her stomach seize. She cannot bear it.

Now, Martha lives in a house that feels smaller than it used to. She avoids driving after dusk. In fact, she avoids driving at all. Her husband drives her to church and to the market, the muscles in her legs jump with tension the whole time. She grips the door handle, her eyes fixed on the road ahead, scanning for headlights that might be approaching too fast. When a car honks nearby, she flinches as though the sound has hit her. She cannot sit with her back to a door in a restaurant. She cannot sleep unless the bedroom window is covered completely, because the streetlamp outside casts a shadow that reminds her of the headlights.

Her dreams have turned violent. Twice a week, she wakes gasping, her nightgown soaked, convinced she is still inside the overturned car. She hears the creak of metal, feels the wet mud against her cheek. Her husband reaches for her, but she does not always recognize him at first. She sees a stranger, and she screams. He has learned to stay still and speak her name softly until her eyes clear.

She used to love sitting on the veranda in the evenings, listening to the children play. Now the sound of their laughter startles her. She cannot tolerate surprise. She has stopped answering the phone after dark, because the ring is too sudden. She has stopped visiting the clinic, even though the nurses ask for her advice. The smell of antiseptic and the sight of the delivery room—bright lights, sterile instruments—bring back the feeling of being trapped, of metal pressing against her ribs. She tells herself she is just old, just tired.

Her husband says she is not the same woman he married. She knows this is true. She has become irritable, snapping at him for small things—the way he clears his throat, the way he leaves the door ajar. She feels guilty afterward, but the guilt turns into a heavy fog that follows her through the day. She no longer believes she is capable of helping anyone. She fails to see a future that holds anything but vigilance and waiting.

When she walks to the garden, she avoids the road. She takes the long way, through the neighbors’ plots, even though it pains her knees. She tells herself it is sensible, but she knows it is fear. The fear has become a second shadow, one that never leaves her alone.
